body:
Per https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2925 I'd like to align SMS use more towards the latest revision of NIST 800-63b R4. My suggestion is:

_6.6.1 Verify that PSTN-delivered OTPs (phone or SMS) are offered only alongside stronger options such as app-based TOTP/HOTP generators with clear risk disclosure to users, are prohibited for Level 3 applications, and that each single-use code expires within 10 minutes and is sent only after the verifier has securely bound the number, checked for high-risk carrier events (e.g., SIM swaps or porting), and applied heightened scrutiny due to the inherent weakness of SMS-based MFA._

comments.body:
The requirement and the section text as it stands at the moment:

---

Unsafe out-of-band authentication mechanisms such as e-mail and VOIP are not permitted. PSTN and SMS authentication are currently considered to be ["restricted" authentication mechanisms](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b01) by NIST and should be deprecated in favor of push notifications or similar. NIST SP 800-63B [§ 5.1.3.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#-5133-authentication-using-the-public-switched-telephone-network) provides guidance if telephone or SMS out-of-band authentication absolutely have to be supported.

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.6.1** | Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when alternate stronger methods (such as push notifications) are also offered and when the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.7.1 |

The August 2024 revision 4 to NIST 800-63b made some subtle changes.

1) push is no longer in favor
3) VOIP is now acceptable 

I can give you the exact citations and more clarification a little bit later if you like.

On VOIP: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators

**Transfer of the secret from the primary to the secondary channel**
As shown in [Fig. 3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#fig-3), the verifier SHALL display a random authentication secret to the claimant via the primary channel. It SHALL then wait for the secret to be returned via the secondary channel from the claimant’s out-of-band authenticator. **_The verifier MAY additionally display an address, such as a phone number or VoIP address, for the claimant to use in addressing its response to the verifier._**

On Push: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators

A third method of out-of-band authentication compares secrets received from the primary and secondary channels and requests approval on the secondary channel. This method is no longer considered acceptable because it increased the likelihood that the subscriber would approve an authentication request without actually comparing the secrets as required. This has been observed with “authentication fatigue” attacks where an attacker (claimant) would generate many out-of-band authentication requests to the subscriber, who might approve one to eliminate the annoyance. **_For this reason, an authenticator that receives a push notification from the verifier and simply asks the claimant to approve the transaction (even if they provide some additional information about the authentication) does not meet the requirements of this section._**

So I would suggest several changes here:

First the section text change suggestion (notably, VOIP is now permitted and push is not based on MFA fatigue). I also suggest we update the references to point to the latest (sp800-63b Revision 4).

**Unsafe out-of-band authentication mechanisms such as e-mail and push notifications are not permitted.** PSTN and SMS authentication are currently considered to be ["restricted" authentication mechanisms](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#restricted) by NIST and should be deprecated in favor of stronger methods. NIST SP 800-63B Revision 4 [§ 3.1.3.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#pstnOOB) provides guidance if telephone or SMS out-of-band authentication absolutely have to be supported.

As for the requirement, I suggest:

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.6.1** | Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when alternate stronger methods (such as app based TOTP generators) are also offered and when the service provides information on their security risks to users. If SMS is used, each code should be single-use, should expire within 10 minutes and should be sent only after the verifier has securely bound the number and checked for high-risk carrier events (e.g., SIM swaps or porting).  For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.7.1 |

For push notifications we have do have [6.6.4](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/pull/3090/commits/d9c4a102773a29e96e23cff15814b0e2643f6ff4) which is designed to address push fatigue:

"_Verify that, where push notifications are used for multi-factor authentication, rate limiting is used to prevent push bombing attacks. Number matching may also mitigate this risk._"

I am a little reluctant to ban it altogether but I will have a think about it.

> If SMS is used, each code should be single-use, should expire within 10 minutes

We have requirements around this in section [6.5](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x15-V6-Authentication.md#v65-general-multi-factor-authentication-requirements).

> should be sent only after the verifier has securely bound the number

As in, they are sending to a verified number? If so, that seems like a sensible precaution.

> checked for high-risk carrier events (e.g., SIM swaps or porting). 

How would an application achieve that?

> For push notifications we have do have [6.6.4](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/pull/3090/commits/d9c4a102773a29e96e23cff15814b0e2643f6ff4) which is designed to address push fatigue:

That's very reasonable. And it maps to https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#out-of-band-verifiers well. 

> I am a little reluctant to ban it altogether but I will have a think about it.

I'm with that too, the main mitigation is rate limiting like we have in 6.6.4.

> > If SMS is used, each code should be single-use, should expire within 10 minutes
> 
> We have requirements around this in section [6.5](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x15-V6-Authentication.md#v65-general-multi-factor-authentication-requirements).

cool

> > should be sent only after the verifier has securely bound the number
> 
> As in, they are sending to a verified number? If so, that seems like a sensible precaution.

Exactly, there needs to be a SMS verification step first during phone number registration before it can be accepted.

> > checked for high-risk carrier events (e.g., SIM swaps or porting).
> 
> How would an application achieve that?

You can querying a carrier‑intelligence service each time you’re about to send an SMS or voice OTP:

* **Twilio Lookup – SIM Swap** returns the timestamp of the last SIM change for the phone number.
* **Telesign Phone ID / SIM Swap** returns a Boolean flag (recent swap yes/no) with a time‑to‑live value.
* **Prove Trust Score** returns a 0‑100 reputation score that drops sharply when a recent SIM swap or port‑out is detected.

1. Call one of the APIs just before you generate the OTP.
2. If the API shows a SIM swap or port‑out within the last 24–72 hours (or the Trust Score is below your chosen threshold), block the SMS/voice path or step the user up to a stronger authenticator.
3. If no recent swap is detected and the Trust Score is acceptable, proceed with the OTP.

> * **Prove Trust Score** returns a 0‑100 reputation score that drops sharply when a recent SIM swap or port‑out is detected.

> 1. Call one of the APIs just before you generate the OTP.
> 2. If the API shows a SIM swap or port‑out within the last 24–72 hours (or the Trust Score is below your chosen threshold), block the SMS/voice path or step the user up to a stronger authenticator.
> 3. If no recent swap is detected and the Trust Score is acceptable, proceed with the OTP.

This feels a little bit too complex for L2 and then for L3 it forbids SMS anyway.

I would therefore suggest the following:


---

Unsafe out-of-band authentication mechanisms such as e-mail and VOIP are not permitted. PSTN and SMS authentication are currently considered to be ["restricted" authentication mechanisms](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-FAQ/#q-b01) by NIST and should be deprecated in favor of code generators or similar. NIST SP 800-63B [§ 5.1.3.3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html#-5133-authentication-using-the-public-switched-telephone-network) provides guidance if telephone or SMS out-of-band authentication absolutely have to be supported. NIST has recently provided guidance which [discourages the use of push notifications](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/#fig-3). Whilst this section does not do so, it is important to be aware of the risks of "push bombing".

| # | Description | Level | #v5.0.be |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: |
| **6.6.1** | Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when the phone number has previously been validated, alternate stronger methods (such as Time based One-time Passwords) are also offered, and the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options. | 2 | v5.0.be-2.7.1 |

> This feels a little bit too complex for L2 and then for L3 it forbids SMS anyway.

I think this is *baseline* security for SMS use and it takes very little time to code. It's actually very trivial to implement.

Pretty sure that requires signing up with one of those three services, no? Not just a question of coding.

Maybe we can note this in the section text that if you're still allowing SMS at L3, you should definitely have this mitigating control

> Pretty sure that requires signing up with one of those three services, no? Not just a question of coding.

It's fairly trivial to sign up for these services. They are simple REST API's with simple output. 

The whole point if this is - SMS is very weak as a control - and verifying high risk carrier events is a quick, easy and effective way to ensure the phone number is not compromised when you depend on this kind of control.

From  https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-63B-4.2pd.pdf (2024)

Section 3.1.3.3 : Authentication Using the Public Switched Telephone Network (2024 latest revision) 

_Verifiers SHOULD consider risk indicators (e.g., device swap, SIM change, number porting, or other abnormal behavior) before using the PSTN to deliver an out-of-band authentication secret._


And this was part of NIST 800-63b since 2017.
Rev. 3 (2017), § 5.1.3.3 “Authentication using the Public Switched Telephone Network

_Verifiers SHOULD consider risk indicators such as device swap, SIM change, number porting, or other abnormal behavior before using the PSTN to deliver an out‑of‑band authentication secret._

> It's fairly trivial to sign up for these services. They are simple REST API's with simple output.

Having seen what some companies have to go through to sign up for a new service, I politely dissent :)

> _Verifiers SHOULD consider risk indicators (e.g., device swap, SIM change, number porting, or other abnormal behavior) before using the PSTN to deliver an out-of-band authentication secret._

In addition to my general feeling that this is not straightforward to achieve, the use of the word "SHOULD" is NIST's way of saying that this is a recommendation, not a requirement.

We could have this in our recommendations section but I think it would be more powerful in the section text.

As this change is getting a little complicated, I have opened a draft PR which hopefully makes it easier to see the proposed enhancements #3105
